sections.title: The single-particle states as basis states

keyResults.name: Slater determinant and permanent (fermions, bosons)
keyResults.note: Eqs. (1.23)-(1.26). Fermions: determinant (sign of the permutation). Bosons: permanent (no sign). The fermion version vanishes when two labels coincide (Pauli). The 1/sqrt(N!) prefactor is for normalized states with all labels different. In general (footnote 2) the normalization is 1/(sqrt(N!) prod_nu sqrt(n_nu!)), where n_nu counts how often state nu appears. For fermions n_nu! = 1, and for bosons the factor is needed when a state is multiply occupied.

questions.prompt: Which relation defines the fermion annihilation and creation operators?
questions.solution: Fermions obey anticommutators, Eq. (1.52). The commutator form is the boson rule (1.41). The anticommutator of two annihilators vanishes, and $c^\dagger c$ is the occupation number, not 1.

questions.prompt: Write the kinetic energy and the Fourier component $\hat\rho_\sigma(q)$ of free electrons in the plane-wave basis.
questions.solution:
$$\hat T=\sum_{k\sigma}\varepsilon_k\,c^\dagger_{k\sigma}c_{k\sigma},\qquad \varepsilon_k=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m},$$
$$\hat\rho_\sigma(q)=\sum_k c^\dagger_{k\sigma}c_{k+q\,\sigma}.$$
The density operator changes the momentum by q, so it creates particle-hole pairs.

questions.prompt: For $\hat H=\sum_{ij}a^\dagger_i h_{ij}a_j$ with $h$ hermitian, what must the unitary $U$ in $\alpha_i=\sum_j U_{ij}a_j$ satisfy so that $\hat H=\sum_i\epsilon_i\alpha^\dagger_i\alpha_i$?
questions.solution:
Write $a=U^\dagger\alpha$, so $a^\dagger=\alpha^\dagger U$ and $\hat H=\alpha^\dagger(UhU^\dagger)\alpha$.
The condition is
$$UhU^\dagger=\mathrm{diag}(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\dots).$$
Equivalently, the $i$-th row $u_i$ of $U$ satisfies $u_i h=\epsilon_i u_i$. Because $U$ is unitary, the new $\alpha_i$ obey the same canonical algebra as the $a_i$, Eq. (1.65).

questions.prompt: Tight-binding model: $\hat H=-t\sum_{j,\delta}c^\dagger_{j+\delta}c_j$ with nearest neighbors $\delta$. Diagonalize it for a 1D ring of $N$ sites with lattice constant $a$ and for a 2D square lattice (Book Exercise 1.4).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 1.4. Use $c_j=N^{-1/2}\sum_k e^{ikja}c_k$ with $k=2\pi n/(Na)$ in the first Brillouin zone. Then
$$\sum_j c^\dagger_{j+\delta}c_j=\sum_k e^{-ik\delta a}c^\dagger_k c_k,$$
because the sum over $j$ gives $\delta_{kk'}$. Summing over the two neighbors $\delta=\pm a$ in 1D:
$$\hat H=\sum_k\varepsilon_k c^\dagger_kc_k,\qquad \varepsilon_k=-2t\cos ka.$$
In 2D, each direction contributes its own cosine:
$$\varepsilon_{\mathbf k}=-2t\left(\cos k_xa+\cos k_ya\right).$$
For $t>0$ the band minimum is at $k=0$ and the bandwidth is $4t$ in 1D and $8t$ in 2D. The Hamiltonian is diagonal in $k$ because it is translation invariant.

questions.prompt: Show that the Yukawa potential $V(r)=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}e^{-k_s r}$ has Fourier transform $V_q=\frac{e^2}{\epsilon_0(q^2+k_s^2)}$, and recover the Coulomb $V_q$ for $k_s\to0$ (Book Exercise 1.6).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 1.6. Write $e_0^2=e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0$. Use spherical coordinates with $\mathbf q$ along the polar axis. The angular integral gives $\int d\cos\theta\,d\phi\,e^{-iqr\cos\theta}=4\pi\,\sin(qr)/(qr)$, so
$$V_q=\int d^3r\,e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}V(r)=\frac{4\pi e_0^2}{q}\int_0^\infty dr\,e^{-k_sr}\sin(qr).$$
The $r^2$ from the volume element cancels the $1/r$ in the potential. The remaining radial integral is elementary:
$$\int_0^\infty dr\,e^{-k_sr}\sin(qr)=\frac{q}{q^2+k_s^2}.$$
Hence $V_q=4\pi e_0^2/(q^2+k_s^2)=e^2/[\epsilon_0(q^2+k_s^2)]$. Setting $k_s\to0$ gives $e^2/(\epsilon_0 q^2)$, the Coulomb result of Eq. (1.102).

questions.prompt: Bogoliubov transformation for fermions. $\hat H=E_0(a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b)+E_1(a^\dagger b^\dagger+ba)$ with $a=u\alpha-v\beta^\dagger$, $b=u\beta+v\alpha^\dagger$, $u,v$ real. Find the conditions on $u,v$ and the diagonal form of $\hat H$ (Book Exercise 1.7).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 1.7. The anticommutators $\{a,a^\dagger\}=1$ and $\{b,b^\dagger\}=1$ with $\{\alpha,\alpha^\dagger\}=\{\beta,\beta^\dagger\}=1$ give $u^2+v^2=1$.

Insert the transformation. Using $\alpha\beta=-\beta\alpha$ and $\alpha\alpha^\dagger=1-\alpha^\dagger\alpha$:
$$a^\dagger a+b^\dagger b=(u^2-v^2)(\alpha^\dagger\alpha+\beta^\dagger\beta)+2v^2-2uv(\alpha^\dagger\beta^\dagger+\beta\alpha)$$
$$a^\dagger b^\dagger+ba=(u^2-v^2)(\alpha^\dagger\beta^\dagger+\beta\alpha)+2uv(\alpha^\dagger\alpha+\beta^\dagger\beta-1)$$

Cancelling the pair terms $(\alpha^\dagger\beta^\dagger+\beta\alpha)$ requires
$$E_1(u^2-v^2)-2uvE_0=0.$$
With $u=\cos t$, $v=\sin t$ this is $E_1\cos2t=E_0\sin2t$, so $\tan2t=E_1/E_0$. Let $\lambda=\sqrt{E_0^2+E_1^2}$, so $\cos2t=E_0/\lambda$ and $\sin2t=E_1/\lambda$. The diagonal coefficient is
$$E_0\cos2t+E_1\sin2t=\lambda.$$
Result: $\hat H=\lambda(\alpha^\dagger\alpha+\beta^\dagger\beta)+\text{const}$, with the constant from the $2v^2E_0-2uvE_1$ terms.
